🐛 Bug
Pytorch crashes during the forward operation of a network, printing no stack trace, only 'Illegal instruction'. This is originally happened in the tutorial linked here: https://pytorch.org/tutorials/beginner/blitz/neural_networks_tutorial.html#sphx-glr-beginner-blitz-neural-networks-tutorial-py
I expect this was due to my old AMD CPU (Phenom II X6 1055T). Compiling pytorch locally (version 1.8.0a0+2ab74a4) results in that tutorial working. However, the following tutorial (https://pytorch.org/tutorials/beginner/blitz/cifar10_tutorial.html#sphx-glr-beginner-blitz-cifar10-tutorial-py) still produces the 'Illegal instruction' message. This appears to be due to the network size.
To Reproduce
Steps to reproduce the behavior:

Use an old CPU (I'm not really sure what features need to be missing - I have an AMD Phenom II X6 1055T), compile pytorch from scratch.
Run the code below. It should print a tensor.
Change the size of at least one of the convolution kernels from 3 to 5. It should now print 'Illegal Instruction.'

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F
import numpy as np


class Net(nn.Module):
    
    def __init__(self):
        super(Net, self).__init__()
        # 1 input channel, 6 output channels, 3x3 convolution
        self.conv1 = nn.Conv2d(3, 6, 3)
        self.conv2 = nn.Conv2d(6, 16, 3)
        # Fully connexted layers: y = Wx + b
        self.fc1 = nn.Linear(16*6*6, 120)
        self.fc2 = nn.Linear(120, 84)
        self.fc3 = nn.Linear(84, 10)
        
    def forward(self, x):
        # Max pooling over a 2x2 window
        x = F.max_pool2d(F.relu(self.conv1(x)), (2, 2))
        x = F.max_pool2d(F.relu(self.conv2(x)), 2)
        x = x.view(-1, self.num_flat_features(x))
        x = F.relu(self.fc1(x))
        x = F.relu(self.fc2(x))
        x = self.fc3(x)
        return x
        
    def num_flat_features(self, x):
        size = x.size()[1:]  # Drop the batch dimension
        num_features = 1
        for s in size:
            num_features *= s
        return num_features


net = Net()
print(net)

input = torch.randn(1, 3, 32, 32)
out = net(input)
print(out)

Expected behavior
I expected the 'Illegal Instruction' message to no longer happen with a locally compiled pytorch.

Proposal for stricter backward compatibility in function schema checks
Currently, there is a backwards compatibility check for the python API which follows python rules. This can be an issue for the C++ API, since the python rules are too permissive for C++ backward compatibility, where only positional arguments (no named args) are available.
This proposal is for going from the more permissive Python-derived rules (see Current backwards-compatibility) to new stricter C++ derived rules (see New backwards-compatibility).
Current backwards-compatibility
A function is backwards compatible if:

The function's structure of old and new match (e.g. name, overload name, etc.).
The new function has a backward compatible argument for every positional argument in the old function.
All new positional arguments (not present in old) appear afterwards (i.e. appended to the list of positional arguments) and either match a kwarg by name and compatibility (i.e. old kwarg becoming positional) or provides a default value.
-- E.g. f_new(a, b, c=1) => f_old(a, b); f_new(a, c=1, *, b) => f_old(a, *, b); f_new(a, b, *, c) => f_old(a, *, b, c)
The new function has a matching backward compatible kwarg for every kwarg in the old function, and all the kwargs in the old function have a matching kwarg or positional argument (per the rule above).
All new kwargs (not present in old) provide a default value.
-- E.g. f_new(a, b, *, c) => f_old(a, *, b, c); f_new(a, *, c, b) => f_old(a, *, b, c); f_new(a, *, b, c, d=1) => f_old(a, *, b, c)

New backwards-compatibility
A function is backwards compatible if:

[Function structure] The new schema's name, overload-name, varargs, and return arity are the same.
[Output Narrowing] The new schema's output type must be the same class or inherit from the old schema's output type.
[Argument count] The new schema must have at least as many arguments as the old schema (considering the list of positional and kwargs).
[Arg Compatibility] Every argument in the old schema has a corresponding argument in the new schema that:
-- is at the same position.
-- has the same name.
-- is either positional, or kwarg and the old argument was kwarg.
-- has the same type, or the old argument's type inherits from the new argument's type.
E.g.
OK    f_new(a, b, c=1) => f_old(a, b)
NOK   f_new(a, c=1, *, b) => f_old(a, *, b)
OK    f_new(a, b, *, c) => f_old(a, *, b, c)
NOK   f_new(a, *, b, c) -> f_old(a, b, *, c)
NOK   f_new(a, *, c, b) => f_old(a, *, b, c)
OK    f_new(a, *, b, c, d=1) => f_old(a, *, b, c)

Memory management for tensor expressions is currently done with memory arenas. That is, whenever an object is created it registers itself in an arena and the object is kept alive as long as the arena is alive. When the arena gets destructed, it deletes all objects registered in it.
For a class to use this memory management mechanism it need to be derived from KernelScopedObject. Most of our classes are like that (see e.g.

         Line 105
      in
      de3a480
    
  
  
    

        
          
           class Tensor : KernelScopedObject { 
        
    
  

), but we forgot one of the classes: Placeholder (see 
  
    
      pytorch/torch/csrc/jit/tensorexpr/tensor.h
    
    
         Line 160
      in
      de3a480
    
  
  
    

        
          
           class Placeholder { 
        
    
  

)
The task is to fix that. The change itself is trivial but it will require a lot of (mostly mechanical) changes in our tests, since after the change we would need to create Placeholder objects with a new instead of allocating them on the stack.

🐛 Bug
Instance norm computes statistics and normalizes tensor along its spatial dimensions. If tensor has just 1 element in spatial dimension, then the mean value is this element itself and variance computed by InstanceNorm layer is 0. In PyTorch realization, the value of normalized tensor will be silently computed as 0, since a small eps value is added to variance before division.
The bug is that instance norm layer does not work silently and throws out an error about dimensions when batch size is 1 and dimensions are H, W= (1, 1). However, if batch size is > 1 and dimensions are the same H, W = (1, 1), it works fine. I do not think it should be any difference between this two cases, since in both statistics are computed on (1, 1)-sized tensor and for both cases normalization is ambiguous.
To Reproduce
import torch as th
import torch.nn as nn

layer = nn.InstanceNorm2d(3)
layer.eval()

layer(th.rand(1, 3, 2, 2)) # works fine - expected 
layer(th.rand(2, 3, 1, 1)) # works fine - expected for silent behavior
layer(th.rand(1, 3, 1, 1)) # error - not expected for silent behavior

Stack trace:

ValueError                                Traceback (most recent call last)
 in ()
8     print(layer(th.rand(2, 3, 1, 1))) # works fine
9 layer(th.rand(1, 3, 2, 2)) # works fine
---> 10 layer(th.rand(1, 3, 1, 1)) # error in eval mode

721         else:
--> 722             result = self.forward(*input, **kwargs)
723         for hook in itertools.chain(
724                 _global_forward_hooks.values(),

55         return F.instance_norm(
56             input, self.running_mean, self.running_var, self.weight, self.bias,
---> 57             self.training or not self.track_running_stats, self.momentum, self.eps)
58

2033                 running_var=running_var, weight=weight, bias=bias,
2034                 use_input_stats=use_input_stats, momentum=momentum, eps=eps)
-> 2035     _verify_batch_size(input.size())
2036     return torch.instance_norm(
2037         input, weight, bias, running_mean, running_var,
~/anaconda3/lib/python3.6/site-packages/torch/nn/functional.py in _verify_batch_size(size)
1993         size_prods *= size[i + 2]
1994     if size_prods == 1:
-> 1995         raise ValueError('Expected more than 1 value per channel when training, got input size {}'.format(size))
1996

ValueError: Expected more than 1 value per channel when training, got input size torch.Size([1, 3, 1, 1])

Expected behavior
If silent behavior is the case, then evaluating InstanceNorm layer on tensor with batch size 1 and spatial size 1 should not throw the error, especially in eval mode. Solution is simple: _verify_batch_size(input.size()) call should be excluded from nn.functional.instance_norm(), since InstanceNorm layer has nothing about batch size.
If silent behavior is not the case, both should throw out an error about dimensions. Error text should be reconsidered, since it tells about training mode, even when layer stays in eval mode.

🚀 High-level Event Tracing
Over time we've received requests from community to provide additional information in profiler traces, including:

High-level events like 'start of a new epoch' or 'another mini-batch iteration'
Data loader activity, e.g. denoting data loader related time ranges (e.g. reading/processing new minibatch)
Tracing activity of optimizers

This feature proposal is primarily for the training, driven by the python program.
(We should keep in mind though that some or all of the model can be run by TorchScript runtime)
Motivation
The motivation is to provide more information in the profiler trace. We currently show three types of ranges in the trace:

c10/aten ops
torchscript model methods/functions
user defined (record_function context manager in python/TS) ranges

For all ranges in the trace we save start/end time, (optionally) input arguments shape, and some extra info (e.g. device).
Pitch
The idea is to add more places inside PyTorch that automatically report themselves to the profiler's trace/stats.
Note: since this is supposed to be used by external tools, the changes proposed here are bound by the backward compatibility requirements.
How this could be implemented:

For high-level training loops events: extend autograd.profiler context manager by adding a predicate parameter, e.g.

   with profiler.profile(
      activities,
      # more args,
      enable_pred =
         enable_when(
            skip_first=20,
            count=5,
            repeat_every=1000,
            warmup=3) as prof:

      for iter in range(N):
         with record_function("iteration " + str(iter)):
            run(minibatch[iter])
         prof.next_minibatch()

The exact API may change, but the main idea is to allow users to notify profiler about high-level semantic events, s.t. next minibatch or next epoch using existing profiler context manager.
Note on the predicate semantics: predicate param is not strictly required by this proposal, but they work together: the purpose of predicate function is to determine on what iterations to run profiler and on what not to run it (we want to enable profiler only on small % of iterations, but we want a uniform coverage and statistics of training process).
If we add API like prof.next_minibatch() this will also allow us to add 'next minibatch' (and also potentially other events like 'next epoch') into the trace.
Note: concepts of 'next minibatch' or 'next epoch' are high-level and ultimately determined by the user, so we allow user to explicitly mark them by e.g. prof.next_minibatch().

For dataloaders:

for torch.utils.data.IterableDataset.__iter__(): wrap internals into `with record_function(LABEL)`

for torch.utils.data.Dataset. __getitem__(): same

Implementation options:

using predetermined string names ("DataLoader__MyDataLoader_getitem") in record_function context manager
allow record_function to take a second param, a user-defined constant (e.g. DATALOADER) in addition to the name of the range (e.g. name of the dataloader class)
hardcode certain types of user event and subclass record_function class (dataloader_record_function with DATALOADER hardcoded into)

Alternatives
There's always an alternative in the form of manual usage of Python's record_function context manager: though at the same time, it has to be used explicitly by the user (in the user's model code) to manually label any piece of code by wrapping it in record_function context manager.
At the same time, carefully exposing some of the internal events, by default in profiler trace, would make it easier for users, and also external tools, to get a fuller picture of the training process.
Notes
Some extra functionality not discussed in this doc:

Automatic registering of eager/script module's 'forward' calls, other eager function calls; tensor-level events.

🐛 Bug
Hi,
I started by posting a question in the forums here: https://discuss.pytorch.org/t/statically-linking-to-libtorch-but-also-needing-the-shared-library-libcaffe2-nvrtc-so/97166/2
But was asked to also post it here as well, so that why I'm writing this now.
I’m building a plugin for a commercial software application that is internally using libtorch. This plugin, which is in the form of a shared library (.so file), is statically linking libtorch (i.e. it’s baking all of it into it’s own so-file). The only libraries that are dynamically linked against are the CUDA libs and some standard system libraries of course. This plugin needs to be portable to other systems without the need to install lots of dependencies (CUDA is fine to be needed as an additional install).
Everything works, except I can’t get my shared library to not also need the torch library “libcaffe2_nvrtc.so”. Since it doesn’t exist a static version of this library “libcaffe2_nvrtc.a”, I can’t seem to get around it. Is there a way to not have libtorch dynamically depend on this library and still have GPU support? I can build libtorch with CPU support only, and then I don’t have the problem, but I need the GPU acceleration.
My guess here is that the libcaffe2_nvrtc library can’t be made static since it directly depends on CUDA which doesn’t exist statically, but that is only my guess, I and would like somebody more knowledgeable to confirm that this is the case. If so, I guess I just have to live with being forced to also distribute the file “libcaffe2_nvrtc.so” together with my plugin, right? Any other suggestions or solutions to get around this issue?
Cheers, David

Compile pytorch statically with CUDA support (-DBUILD_SHARED_LIBS=OFF -DUSE_MKLDNN=OFF -DUSE_CUDA=ON)
You do get all the static libraries as .a-files of course. But the "libcaffe2_nvrtc" library does still become a dynamic .so-file.

All other libtorch dependencies are successfully baked into the new executable/dynamic library and will work. It will also work with CUDA and GPU acceleration.

That all libtorch libraries compiled to be static .a-files, that I could link against to not need extra dynamic library files on the side when I distribute my .so-file to other systems (where libtorch is not installed).

Currently,  pytorch supports quantized implementations of leaky relu and sigmoid. For the case of sigmoid, the outputs of the quantized module are quantized over the range [0,1]. For the leaky_relu, the scale and zero-point of the input is used to define the range for the output.  This is not modeled during quantization aware training.
A possible solution is to define:

nn.qat.sigmoid module: that has a fake-quantize module at the output with a fixed scale and zero-point.
nn.qat.leaky_relu module: Needs to have a fake-quantize module at the output with scale and zero-point matching that of the input.  This may not be possible in eager mode as we do not know the input scale and zero-point, but should be possible with fx quantization.

🐛 Bug

I'm trying to implement a tied autoencoder where the weights of the decoder are simply the transpose of the encoder. However, I got a CUDA crash when invoking .backward(), but it works fine on CPU. An MWE and workaround are provided below.
To Reproduce
The MWE is as follows:
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F
import torch.optim as optim


class FakeAE(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.enc_w = nn.Parameter(torch.Tensor(3, 5))
        self.dec_w = self.enc_w.T

        nn.init.normal_(self.enc_w)

    def encode(self, data):
        return F.linear(data, self.enc_w)

    def decode(self, data):
        # return F.linear(data, self.enc_w.T)  # workaround the error
        return F.linear(data, self.dec_w)

    def forward(self, data):
        return self.decode(self.encode(data))


def main():
    device = 'cuda'
    # device = 'cpu'  # works!
    ae = FakeAE().to(device)
    criterion = nn.MSELoss()
    optimizer = optim.SGD(ae.parameters(), lr=1)

    data = torch.rand((2, 5)).to(device)
    rec = ae(data)
    loss = criterion(data, rec)

    optimizer.zero_grad()
    loss.backward()
    optimizer.step()

I want to record some information into log-file and print it in console at the same time. So I use two logger handlers.
I also want to plot some figures so I use Tensorboard to make it.
However, I found that after initializing the SummaryWriter, the 2nd handler always disappeared and all log messages couldn't be displayed in console!
To Reproduce
Steps to reproduce the behavior:

You can reproduce the behavior by the following simple code:

import logging
import os

from torch.utils.tensorboard import SummaryWriter


class FileFormatter(logging.Formatter):
    def __init__(self, *args, **kw):
        super().__init__(*args, **kw)

    def format(self, record):
        s = super().format(record)
        s = s.replace('\033[K', '').replace('\033[1A', '')
        return s


class ConsoleFormatter(logging.Formatter):
    def __init__(self, *args, **kw):
        red_level = getattr(logging, kw.pop('red_level', 'WARNING').upper())
        super().__init__(*args, **kw)
        if not isinstance(red_level, int):
            raise ValueError(f'Invalid log RED_LEVEL')
        self.red_level = red_level

    def format(self, record):
        s = super().format(record)
        if record.levelno >= self.red_level:
            s = f'\033[31m{s}\033[0m'
        return s


def set_log():
    logger = logging.getLogger()
    loglevel = getattr(logging, 'INFO', None)
    logger.setLevel(loglevel)
    log_path = './test/something.log'
    os.makedirs(os.path.dirname(log_path), exist_ok=True)
    fl = logging.FileHandler(filename=log_path)
    fl.setLevel(loglevel)
    fl_formatter = FileFormatter(r'%(asctime)s:%(levelname)s:%(message)s',
                                 datefmt=r'%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S')
    fl.setFormatter(fl_formatter)
    logger.addHandler(fl)

    ch = logging.StreamHandler()
    ch.setLevel(loglevel)
    ch_formatter = ConsoleFormatter(r'%(asctime)s:%(levelname)s:%(message)s',
                                    datefmt=r'%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S', red_level='WARNING')
    ch.setFormatter(ch_formatter)
    logger.addHandler(ch)


def main():
    set_log()
    logging.info('This message is normal.')
    logging.warning('This message is normal. And it is red in Console.')
    train_board = SummaryWriter('what_happened')
    logging.info('This message cannot be displayed in console '
                 'because the 2nd logger handler disappeared '
                 'after initializing the SummaryWriter. '
                 'But it is still written in log-file by the 1st handler.')
    logging.warning('Me too.')


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

🚀 Feature
The SVD based torch.pinverse which works with complex tensors would be great.
Motivation
For low-rank matrices, this is an absolute must. And of course we can use the torch.svd functionality and then write the pseudoinverse ourselves, however this would make life a bit simpler.
Edit
One overarching more issue I've come across is the lack of functionality in PyTorch for complex tensors. Although I would like a pinverse function, I can still take the pseudoinverse of a complex tensor via the SVD. But then I ran into the issue that matrix multiplication of complex tensors is not supported. So I wrote a function to compute complex matmul. Then I went to start training the network and was hit with the warning that complex tensor gradients aren't fully supported. I am running PyTorch 1.6.0 by the way.
So I guess my question would be if these issues are on the radar of the PyTorch team? And have you found that others would like this functionality as well? I, for one, would greatly benefit from full complex tensor support! Thanks for reading!
cc @ezyang @anjali411 @dylanbespalko @vincentqb @vishwakftw @jianyuh @nikitaved @pearu
nodes.title: torch.pinverse for complex tensors and general complex tensor support
